1191.title: Do not steal
1191.howItsDone: Christian teaching on this commandment often extends it to fair wages, honest work and repaying what was taken, and some churches practice restitution as part of repentance, following the example of Zacchaeus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faithfulness: Ruth on the road, refusing to leave. Your line was faithful.

Jericho, and a crowd lining the road. Zacchaeus is a chief tax collector, and rich, and too short to see over anyone, so he runs ahead and climbs a sycamore tree. Jesus stops right under it, calls him by name, and invites himself to stay at his house. The crowd mutters about the company Jesus keeps. And then Zacchaeus stands up and says: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold."

"Thou shalt not steal." It sounds like a commandment about wallets and shoplifting. Scripture keeps pushing it further. Leviticus says: "the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning." Sitting on a worker's pay is a kind of theft. James is fiercer: "the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth." Withheld wages cry out. So stealing can include the invoice you never quite pay, the hours you bill and don't work, the overtime you demand and don't pay for. It can include time: the meeting that eats everyone's afternoon because nobody prepared. And it can include credit: your name on someone else's idea, a compliment you let land on you that belonged to a colleague. Paul gives the cure in a sentence: "Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth." Notice the direction. Not only stop taking. Start giving. That's what Zacchaeus does. The story records no demand from Jesus and no lecture, only Jesus asking to stay at his house, and Zacchaeus offers to hand things back, four times over. Then Jesus says, "This day is salvation come to this house." In this story, giving it back is part of what that day looks like.

Look back over the last week or month: whose idea did you use, whose work made yours look good, who covered for you or fixed the thing you got thanked for? Let one name come up, and think how you'd say it out loud, in a meeting, an email, or straight to them. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name.
Do not steal. Not taking what isn't yours, including wages, time and credit, and giving back what was taken.
Your line: give it back. Wages, time and credit all count, not only the wallet. Until tomorrow.

1192.title: Truthful witness
1192.hook: no false witness: gossip, spin, half-truths
1192.howItsDone: Some Christians learn this commandment in catechism classes and examine their speech by it before confession or in personal prayer; Luther's Small Catechism and the Catholic catechism both apply it to gossip, slander and harmful talk about people who are absent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, do not steal, and the quiet thefts tucked inside it: wages, time, credit. Your line was give it back.

A sentence drifts across a lunch table: she's not really sick, you know. Nobody swore an oath. Nothing in it is quite a lie. And by evening a few people see her a little differently. Some readers hear a courtroom behind today's commandment, a place where one witness could ruin a neighbor's life. The King James Bible gives it like this: "Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour." But Christian teachers have carried it out of the courtroom and into every room where one person describes another who isn't there to answer. The lunch table counts.

Start with how Proverbs describes gossip: "The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly." Gossip isn't loud, but the wound goes deep. Proverbs also lists a false witness that speaketh lies among the things the Lord hates, right beside the one who sows discord among brothers. So a lie about someone is never just a private slip. It splits people apart. Now the harder part: what if the thing you say is true? The Catholic catechism names a sin called detraction: making known someone's real faults to people who had no need to know, without good reason. The fact is true. The harm is real anyway. Martin Luther, in his Small Catechism, turns the commandment around. It isn't only don't lie about your neighbor. It's defend your neighbor, speak well of them, and put the kindest reading on what they do. Spin and half-truths fail that test, even when every word could be checked. Paul gives the reason underneath it all, in his letter to the Ephesians: "speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another." In Paul's picture, a lie about one member of the body is a lie told to the whole body. A truthful witness, then, is more than someone who avoids lies. It's someone a neighbor would be glad to have in the room when they aren't.

Bring to mind one person you might talk about today, a coworker, a relative, a name in the news, and notice what you'd usually say. Then try Luther's turn: find one true thing you could say in their defense, and just hold it. If you pray, you can use an old line from Psalm 141: "Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips."
Truthful witness. Someone whose words about a neighbor are true, fair and kind, whether that neighbor is in the room or not.
Your line: speak truly. Even about someone who isn't in the room. Rest well.

1193.title: Do not covet
1193.hook: the only commandment about desire alone
1193.howItsDone: Christians learn this commandment with the rest of the Ten Commandments in catechism and Sunday school, and examine themselves by it in prayer; Paul's words on contentment in Philippians 4 are sometimes read alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the truthful witness: no gossip, no spin, no harmful half-truths about someone who isn't there. Your line was speak truly.

House. Wife. Manservant. Maidservant. Ox. Donkey. The commandment piles them up one after another, the way an eye moves down a street, over a fence, into somebody else's yard. And then, as if it knows the list could never be finished, it ends with: anything that is your neighbor's. Read the earlier commandments and they mostly name things a person does: steal, kill, speak falsely. This one names something that can happen without anyone moving a muscle. Some readers point out that it's about desire alone.

Here it is in the King James Bible: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's." Notice what it doesn't forbid. Wanting a house isn't the problem. Wanting your neighbor's house is: the desire that looks at someone else's life and decides it should have been yours. The apostle Paul picks out this commandment when he describes what the law showed him about himself. In his letter to the Romans he writes: "I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet." Some readers put it this way: his hands might stay clean, but his wanting was another matter, and this commandment brought it into the light. So the Christian answer isn't to stop wanting. It's contentment, and Paul is honest that it takes practice. To the Philippians he writes: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." Learned. Not born with it. The letter to the Hebrews gives the ground under it: be content with such things as ye have, for God has said, "I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee." Coveting says my life is short of something, and the neighbor has it. Contentment says what I have is enough, because I'm not left alone with it. It doesn't mean pretending you lack nothing. It means you can see your neighbor's good things and leave them where they are.

Bring to mind one person who has something you've wanted, a house, a job, a marriage, an easy kind of confidence, and notice whatever stirs in you, without scolding it. Then, on each slow breath, wish them well in it: their house kept warm, their work going well. If you pray, you can thank God for what they've been given.
Do not covet. Don't set your desire on what belongs to your neighbor. The commandment that reaches past the hands to the wanting itself.
Your line: enough is enough. Contentment, Paul says, is something learned, not born. See you tomorrow.

1194.title: Faith
1194.hook: the first theological virtue: trust in God, a gift that grows
1194.howItsDone: Christians speak of faith as trust in God that is given and grows; in some churches they profess it together in a creed on Sundays, and some pray the father's words from Mark 9:24 or the apostles' 'increase our faith' in hard moments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, do not covet: the commandment about wanting what's your neighbor's. Your line was enough is enough.

A father has brought his sick son to Jesus's disciples, and they couldn't help. Now Jesus is here, and the father says, if thou canst do any thing, help us. Jesus picks up that little word if. All things are possible, he says, to him that believeth. And the father, in Mark's Gospel, cries out with tears: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Belief and unbelief in one breath, and Jesus heals the boy. A new stretch begins: three gifts Christian teachers call the theological virtues. The first in Paul's list is the one the father was holding onto with both hands.

Paul names the three together at the end of his passage on love, which day 89 met: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three." Christian teachers came to call them theological virtues, because they're aimed at God, and tradition says they're given by God rather than built by effort alone. The Greek word the New Testament uses for faith, pistis, also means trust. Faith here is less a list of ideas you sign and more a hand you put in someone else's. The letter to the Hebrews puts it this way: "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." And it's called a gift. Ephesians says: "by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Christians read that weight differently. Lutheran and Reformed churches tend to stress that last line: through faith, a gift, not earned. Catholic and Orthodox churches tend to stress, with Galatians, faith which worketh by love. Both read both verses. And a gift can grow. In Luke's Gospel the apostles ask Jesus, "Increase our faith." He answers that faith even as small as a grain of mustard seed could tell a tree to be uprooted and planted in the sea. Which brings us back to the father. He didn't wait until his doubt was gone. He brought it along, said so out loud, and asked for help with it. In the story, that was enough to begin.

Find one worry you've been carrying in a closed fist, a child, a test result, money, a decision, name it plainly, and slowly open your hands on your knees, palms up. If you pray, you can hand it over in the father's words, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief; if you don't, just let your hands stay open and notice what it's like not to grip.
Faith. In the New Testament's Greek, pistis: trust in God. Christians call it a gift, and something that can grow.
Your line: trust. Doubt is allowed to come along. I'll be here tomorrow.

1195.title: Hope
1195.hook: hope is not optimism but confidence in God's promise
1195.howItsDone: Christians speak of hope as confidence in God's promises rather than a prediction; Lamentations 3:22–23 is sung in some churches as the hymn 'Great Is Thy Faithfulness', and some Christians use the anchor of Hebrews 6:19 as a symbol of hope.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith: pistis, trust, a gift that can grow, even alongside doubt. Your line was trust.

The city has fallen. The walls are down, the streets are empty, and the poet who wrote the Book of Lamentations doesn't pretend otherwise. For two long chapters and into a third, he weeps. He says God has walled him in, made his chains heavy, shut out his prayer. There is nothing in sight to be optimistic about. And then, right in the middle of the book, the voice turns. Not because anything outside has changed. The rubble is still there. He turns because he remembers something. That turn is the second of the three virtues.

Here's what he remembers, in the King James Bible: "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." His hope doesn't come from the news, or from a feeling that things are looking up. It comes from God's character, and God's promise. That's the difference between optimism and hope as Christians speak of it. Optimism reads the situation and expects it to improve. Hope can read the same situation, see no improvement at all, and still lean forward, because it rests on who God is. Paul puts it bluntly in Romans: "hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for?" If you can already see it, you don't need hope. Hope is for the dark stretch. Then the letter to the Hebrews gives hope its picture, the one in today's line: "Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast." An anchor doesn't stop the storm or calm the water. It holds the ship in place while the storm goes on, so the ship isn't driven onto the rocks. Hope, in this picture, doesn't make the night shorter. It keeps you from being carried off by it.
screen: `HOPE THAT IS SEEN IS NOT HOPE.`

segments.voice: Find one thing you're waiting for that you can't see yet, someone's healing, a reconciliation, a change in yourself that's slow in coming, and name it quietly in one sentence, without measuring the odds. Rest your breath on it, the way an anchor rests on the seabed: heavy, still, holding. If you pray, you can borrow the poet's words: this I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. And if the dark feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

Your line: hope is an anchor. It holds while the storm goes on. Go gently.

1196.title: Love
1196.hook: the greatest virtue, the one that lasts (1 Corinthians 13:13)
1196.howItsDone: Some Christians choose 1 Corinthians 13 for weddings and funerals, and churches in different traditions teach love of God and neighbor as the heart of Christian life, shown in works of mercy and everyday kindness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hope: not a forecast, but an anchor that holds while the storm goes on. Your line was hope is an anchor.

The church in Corinth was arguing. Early in Paul's first letter to them, he says word has reached him that there are contentions among them. Some say they follow Paul, some Apollos, some Peter. Later in the letter they're comparing spiritual gifts: who speaks in tongues, who prophesies, whose gift matters more. And right in the middle of that quarrel, Paul stops and writes the passage on love. It wasn't written for a candlelit ceremony. It was written to a room full of people who were tired of each other. Day 89 met it as love is patient; today, the third virtue, the one Paul calls the greatest.

Open the King James Bible to that chapter and you won't find the word love. You'll find charity. "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up." The old Latin Bible, the Vulgate, has caritas in the same place, and that's today's word. In the Greek Paul wrote, it's agape. Whatever the language, Paul doesn't define love as a feeling. He describes it as behavior: patient, kind, not jealous, not showing off. Some readers hear each line aimed at a Corinthian habit. Then he says the thing that gives love its place above the others: "Charity never faileth." Prophecies will end, he says. Knowledge will pass. And the chapter closes: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." Why the greatest? Paul doesn't spell it out, and readers have offered reasons. One old reading goes like this: faith will one day see what it trusted, and hope will one day have what it waited for, but love has nowhere further to go. It simply continues. That's today's line. And because love is behavior, it has to land somewhere. The first letter of John says it plainly: "let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth." Caritas isn't proved in a speech. It's proved in a dish washed, a call returned, a grudge not mentioned.

Bring one person to mind, ideally someone a little tiring, the way the Corinthians were tiring to each other, and walk through Paul's lines with them in view: patient, where could you wait for them; kind, what one kind thing would actually help? Pick one deed, small and specific. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
Caritas. The Latin word for the love in Paul's chapter, charity in the King James: patient, kind, shown in deeds, and the one that never fails.
Your line: love lasts. The deed can stay quiet, and it still counts. See you tomorrow.

1197.title: Prudence
1197.hook: practical wisdom: the right thing, the right way, at the right time
1197.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox teaching names prudence among the cardinal virtues; some Christians practice it by praying before decisions, seeking counsel and weighing the timing of what they say and do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, caritas: love as behavior, patient and kind, the one Paul says never fails. Your line was love lasts.

"The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going." That's Proverbs, and it could be pinned above every inbox. A text arrives: your package is on hold, tap here and pay a small fee. One person taps before finishing the sentence. Another reads it twice, checks where it came from, and waits. Neither is necessarily smarter. One just looked well to his going. Faith, hope and love were the virtues aimed at God. Now come the four that Christian teachers call the cardinal virtues, the ones for running an ordinary life. The first is prudence.

The four are named together in the Book of Wisdom, which Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include and King James printings place among the Apocrypha. Speaking of wisdom, it says: "for she teacheth temperance and prudence, justice and fortitude." Christian teachers took that list and built on it. Prudence comes first in their order, because it steers the others. It's practical wisdom: knowing the right thing, the right way to do it, and the right time. Not cleverness, and not caution for its own sake. A prudent person can be bold. Jesus sends his disciples out with a strange pairing: "be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves." Sharp-eyed and gentle at once. That's prudence. Ecclesiastes gives the timing part: there is "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak." The same true words can heal at one moment and wound at another. Prudence notices which moment it is. And this closes a week, so look back at what it's steered. Do not steal: give it back. A truthful witness: speak truly. Do not covet: enough is enough. Then faith, trust. Hope, an anchor. Love, the one that lasts. Each needs prudence to land well: knowing when to speak a hard truth, how to give something back without a scene, where a concrete act of love will actually help. The commandments and the virtues say what. Prudence asks how, and when.

Prudence. Practical wisdom: the right thing, the right way, at the right time. The virtue Christian teachers place first, to steer the rest.
